newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's Kim in major reversal on labour law.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's Kim in major reversal on labour law.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam, bowing to public anxiety and damage to the economy, agreed on Tuesday to send a controversial labour law back to parliament in a stunning concession to the opposition.

Kim expressed sorrow for output losses worth billions of dollars through strikes sparked by forced passage of the bill, and said labour strife had defeated the law's aim of revitalising a sluggish economy.
In a meeting with his chief political rivals, Kim also agreed to reopen debate on another controversial law reviving the powers of a once notorious domestic spy agency.

And, in a further about-face, he told heads of three main political parties he would instruct officials to suspend arrest warrants served on strike leaders, seven of whom are sheltering in Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.

Several hundred Roman Catholic nuns and priests, joined by Protestant pastors and Buddhist monks, marched in a protest against the labour law that ended in fist fights with riot police on the way to the cathedral.
The rare protest by clergy representing South Korea's main faiths began with prayers in a Buddhist temple.
The president received guarded approval from opposition leader Kim Dae-jung of the National Congress for New Politics, who welcomed Kim's retreat from his hard line stance.
But the head of a militant union group directing a worker revolt against the law from a tent in the cathedral grounds said he was disappointed.
Kwon Young-kil, head of the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, told a news conference: "Talks today have not solved any of the basic problems".
He said suspending arrest warrants would be "meaningless" unless legal complaints filed against confederation members by corporations suing for damages were dropped.

"Anything can be discussed in parliament again, whether it is the labour law or the law on the Agency for National Security Planning," a spokesman quoted Kim as saying during a lunch meeting in the Presidential Blue House.
Both laws were rammed through parliament in a six-minute dawn session on December 26 with no debate and while opposition deputies slept.
President Kim agreed to the meeting on Monday in a dramatic climbdown. He previously insisted the laws could not be altered and rejected repeated demands by the opposition for dialogue.
But it was clear hard political bargaining still lay ahead, with unions and the opposition adamant the labour law be scrapped, and Kim insisting it could only be revised.

The labour law makes it easier for firms to sack workers and replace strikers. It maintains a partial ban on freedom of union association by delaying recognition of the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions until 2000.
Kim Dae-jung said the president's comments were a step in the right direction, and he even appeared taken aback by the abrupt retreat.

"Today's meeting was not a total solution but there was some advance and President Kim Young-sam showed an attitude of wanting to solve the problems together with opposition parties," he told a news conference.
He said he had complained that the security law would intimidate intellectuals, journalists, farmers, workers and opposition politicians.
The president replied, "then revise the national security law too", according to Kim Dae-jung, who added "I was very surprised at this".

After he took office in 1993, Kim Young-sam clipped the wings of the spy agency that once hounded dissidents and snooped on unionists. The new law restores its powers of investigation that were turned over to prosecutors and police.
The security law is ostensibly aimed at combating subversion from communist North Korea.

The spokesman quoted the president as saying the laws "had made the situation in our economy more difficult, causing public anxiety". The president added: "The purpose of politics is to make people comfortable."
Production losses from more than three weeks of stoppages have been put at more than $3 billion, with export losses estimated at $483 million.

Share prices tumbled on fears President Kim would retreat from a law that economists say is needed to make the labour market more flexible and trim industrial costs. The announcement came after the market closed.
Park In-sang, leader of the officially-sanctioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions, expressed disappointment.

"The patched-up solution to reopen debate on the labour law in parliament falls short of the federation's demand to make the vicious labour law completely void and revised," he said in a statement. "This will not get support from workers."
